how do i choose a dining room color pale.bodyHtml:
Choosing a dining room colour palette is one of those decisions that can feel surprisingly overwhelming — but it doesn't have to be. The best dining room colour palette ideas don't start with a paint chart; they start with the things you already love: a piece of wall art, a favourite fabric, or even the colour of your crockery.

By Mae Osz | Interior Design Consultant & Home Decor Expert with 12+ years of experience.

Have you ever stood in a paint shop holding seventeen sample cards, completely paralysed, wondering why choosing a colour feels harder than assembling flat-pack furniture? I've been there — and so have almost every one of my clients. The good news is that once you start with wall art and decor as your anchor, the whole process gets a lot simpler and a lot more fun.

Quick answer: To choose a dining room colour palette, start with a piece of wall art, a rug, or a fabric you already love and pull two or three colours from it. Then decide whether you want a light and airy feel or something bold and dramatic, and let the room's size and natural light guide how saturated those colours should be.

A dining room colour palette is essentially the full set of colours working together in the space — not just the paint on the walls, but the tones in your furniture, your textiles, your lighting, and your decor accessories. Getting that combination right creates a room that feels intentional rather than thrown together. If you're starting from scratch or refreshing what you have, exploring unique wall art and unique home decor is genuinely one of the best places to find your colour direction before you commit to anything permanent.

List of Contents

  • Best Colours for a Dining Room by Style and Mood
  • Dining Room Colour Combinations and Pairings
  • Accent Walls and Painted Furniture Ideas
  • Light and Airy vs Bold and Dramatic Palette Choices
  • Top Colour Picks by Room Size and Natural Light
  • How Wall Art and Prints Complement a Dining Room Colour Palette
  • Pairing Wall Decor with Specific Paint Colours
  • Colour Palette Ideas by Dining Room Aesthetic
  • Budget-Friendly Ways to Introduce Colour Through Art and Accessories
  • Seasonal and Trend-Led Dining Room Palettes for Right Now
  • Visual Inspiration: Dining Room Colour Styles and Looks
  • More About Building a Dining Room Colour Palette

Best Colours for a Dining Room by Style and Mood

The right colour for your dining room depends entirely on how you want the room to feel. A colour that reads as sophisticated in one home can feel cold and uninviting in another — it's all about the mood you're after and the style of furniture you're working with.

Think about what happens in your dining room most often. Is it quick weekday suppers, Sunday roasts with the family, or dinner parties with friends? The atmosphere you want to create should drive your colour decisions from the start.

[[IMG|dining-room-colour-by-mood-and-style|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome — shelves, wall sconces, a macramé hanging, mirrors — style the walls naturally and lived-in. Scene: A warm, inviting dining room with a round oak table set for an informal family dinner, sage green walls, warm terracotta ceramic tableware, linen curtains in off-white, and a rattan pendant light overhead. A small wooden sideboard holds a potted olive tree. A Black British woman in her early 40s stands at the sideboard arranging flowers in a clay vase, candid and natural.]]

Colour by Style and Mood

  • Warm and welcoming (traditional/country): Terracotta, warm cream, mustard yellow, deep ochre.
  • Cool and calm (contemporary/Scandi): Sage green, dusty blue, warm grey, off-white.
  • Sophisticated and dramatic (maximalist/glam): Deep teal, forest green, midnight navy, aubergine.
  • Fresh and natural (Japandi/biophilic): Stone, warm white, clay, mossy green.
  • Playful and creative (eclectic): Coral, burnt orange, saffron, sunny yellow.
  • Timeless and elegant (classic): Soft white, slate blue, heritage red, charcoal.

I once worked with a client who had a beautiful dark walnut dining table and wanted the room to feel like a proper grown-up space — somewhere that felt different from the rest of the house. We went with a deep, smoky blue-green and paired it with brass light fittings. The transformation was genuinely dramatic, and it didn't require a single piece of new furniture.

Pro Tip: Bring a piece of fabric, a cushion, or even a ceramic bowl from your dining room to the paint shop when you're choosing colours. Seeing the paint chip against something from your actual room is far more useful than comparing chips under shop lighting.

Dining Room Colour Combinations and Pairings

A single colour rarely tells the whole story in a room. The magic happens in the combinations — how two or three colours relate to each other, contrast or complement, and work together across different surfaces and textures.

The simplest way to think about this is to work with a dominant colour (your walls or largest surface), a secondary colour (furniture, curtains, or rug), and an accent colour (smaller decor pieces, candles, artwork details). Keep the ratio roughly 60/30/10 and you'll rarely go wrong.

[[IMG|dining-room-colour-combinations-pairings|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor welcome — a ceramic wall-hung platter, a shelf with plants. Scene: A modern dining room showing a clear 60/30/10 colour palette — deep sage green walls, a natural oak dining table with upholstered dusty rose dining chairs, warm white linen curtains. A terracotta ceramic jug and white candles sit at the centre of the table. A South Asian man in his 30s sits at the table with a coffee, looking thoughtfully towards the window in a candid pose.]]
Primary Colour Secondary Colour Accent Colour Mood
Sage green Warm white Terracotta Natural, grounded
Midnight navy Warm grey Brass / gold Sophisticated, dramatic
Soft blush Cream Dusty mauve Romantic, soft
Charcoal Stone white Warm amber Contemporary, bold
Warm terracotta Cream Forest green Earthy, inviting
Slate blue Linen / natural linen Rusty orange Relaxed, coastal
Pro Tip: If you're nervous about committing to a bold wall colour, start by introducing that colour in your textiles and accessories first. If you still love it after a few weeks, then paint the walls. This approach has saved so many of my clients from expensive repaints.
[[PRODUCT|botanical wall art prints in sage green and terracotta tones]]

Accent Walls and Painted Furniture Ideas

An accent wall is one of the most practical tools in a decorator's kit — it lets you bring a bold, saturated colour into a room without the commitment of painting all four walls. In a dining room, the wall behind a sideboard or buffet is usually the most effective spot.

Painted furniture is another avenue that's wildly underused. A dining table or set of chairs painted in a deep, rich colour can do the same job as an accent wall — and you can always repaint them if you change your mind.

[[IMG|dining-room-accent-wall-painted-furniture|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, contemporary British home styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor welcome — a ceramic wall shelf, a hanging dried flower arrangement. Scene: A dining room with a single deep forest-green accent wall behind a slim marble-top sideboard. The other walls are warm white. A set of painted dark olive dining chairs sits around a light natural oak table. Dried pampas grass in a tall ceramic vase sits on the sideboard. A white British woman in her late 30s is placing a tall candle on the sideboard, in a candid natural pose.]]

Accent Wall and Furniture Painting Ideas

  • Paint the chimney breast or alcove wall in a deep jewel tone while keeping other walls neutral.
  • Use the same colour on both the accent wall and your skirting boards for a more considered, wrapped effect.
  • Paint just the dining chair legs in a contrasting colour (navy legs on a natural wood chair, for instance) — small but impactful.
  • A painted sideboard in sage green or dusty blue instantly anchors the room without touching the walls at all.
  • Try a two-tone wall — paint the lower two-thirds (to dado rail height) in a darker shade and the upper third in a lighter tone.
  • Colour-drenching one corner of a room (walls, trim, and ceiling of that corner in the same shade) creates a cosy, enveloping feel.

A client of mine had a perfectly good sideboard she was about to get rid of because it felt dated. We painted it in a warm terracotta, replaced the handles with brushed brass ones, and it became the focal point of the entire room. She messages me pictures of it regularly — genuinely one of my favourite transformations on a tiny budget.

[[PRODUCT|terracotta and warm-toned abstract wall art prints]]
Real Example: A two-tone wall — darker on the bottom, lighter on top — is a brilliant trick for rooms with low ceilings. The lighter upper tone draws the eye upward and makes the ceiling feel higher, while the darker lower half gives the room a grounded, purposeful feel.

Light and Airy vs Bold and Dramatic Palette Choices

This is the big decision, and it's one where I see people second-guess themselves constantly. Both approaches work brilliantly in a dining room — but they create completely different experiences of the space, and you need to be honest with yourself about which one you actually want to live with.

Light and airy palettes create a sense of space, freshness, and calm. Bold and dramatic palettes create intimacy, warmth, and a sense of occasion. Neither is better — it's entirely about the atmosphere you want to eat and entertain in.

[[IMG|light-airy-vs-bold-dramatic-dining-room|3:2|infographic|Clean minimal educational infographic, plain WHITE background, photoreal, all text solid BLACK. A short centred title near the top: "Light & Airy vs Bold & Dramatic Dining Room Palettes". Then two clearly labelled side-by-side room photos: LEFT labelled "Light & Airy" showing a dining room in soft whites, warm greys and pale sage with natural linen and rattan details; RIGHT labelled "Bold & Dramatic" showing a dining room in deep midnight navy with warm brass accents and rich velvet upholstery. Below each photo, three short bullet labels in solid black text listing the key traits: Left: Open, Fresh, Spacious. Right: Intimate, Warm, Theatrical. Minimal words, generous white space, nothing near the edges. No people, no watermarks.]]

How to Decide Between Light/Airy and Bold/Dramatic

  • Room size: Smaller rooms can handle bold colours beautifully — embracing the cosiness rather than fighting it. Light colours work best in already generous spaces.
  • Natural light: North-facing rooms can feel cold with pale colours; a warm, saturated tone can actually make them feel cosier and more welcoming.
  • How you use the room: If your dining room doubles as a daytime work or study space, lighter palettes are more versatile. For evenings-only entertaining, go bold.
  • Your furniture: Dark, heavy furniture tends to disappear into dark walls (in a good way), while light furniture pops against bold backgrounds.
  • Your personality: Be honest. If you're a cautious decorator who changes their mind often, start lighter. You can always go darker later.
Pro Tip: If you want a bold, dramatic palette but feel nervous, try it on the ceiling first. A deep, rich ceiling colour in an otherwise neutral room creates a cosy, theatrical effect that's far less scary than four dark walls — and the results are usually stunning.

Top Colour Picks by Room Size and Natural Light

Room size and the direction your windows face are two of the most practical constraints in any decorating decision, and they matter enormously in a dining room. The same colour can feel completely different depending on whether the room gets blasting south-facing sun or cool, diffused north-facing light.

Here's how I approach it with every client: we identify which direction the main windows face, how many windows there are, and whether there are any obstructions outside like tall hedges or neighbouring buildings. That tells us a lot before we even look at a paint chip.

[[IMG|dining-room-colour-by-room-size-natural-light|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor welcome — a woven wall hanging, wall-mounted sconces either side of a mirror. Scene: A small north-facing dining room that feels warm and welcoming despite its size, painted in a warm deep terracotta. A round table for two sits in the centre with warm cream linen napkins and a beeswax candle. A large round mirror on the wall bounces light around the room. An East Asian woman in her late 30s and a Black man in his early 40s are seated at the table sharing a casual meal, both laughing naturally and candidly.]]
Room Type Best Colour Choices Colours to Avoid
Small, north-facing Warm terracotta, warm white, soft yellow, deep earthy tones Cool grey, icy blue, stark white
Small, south-facing Soft sage, light blush, warm linen, pale aqua Very dark tones (can feel heavy with strong sun)
Large, north-facing Deep jewel tones, forest green, navy, burnt sienna Very pale, cold shades that make the room feel clinical
Large, south-facing Any colour — lucky you! Bold or light, both work well Nothing to avoid specifically — just ensure tones suit your furniture
Open-plan dining area Consistent neutral base with bold accents in the dining zone Colours that clash with the adjacent living space
Pro Tip: Mirrors are one of the best tricks for making a small, dark dining room feel lighter and larger without changing the colour at all. A round mirror placed opposite a window bounces natural light around the room and adds a decorative element at the same time.
[[PRODUCT|abstract warm-toned artwork for small dining rooms]]

How Wall Art and Prints Complement a Dining Room Colour Palette

This is the bit that most decorating guides completely skip over, and honestly it's the part I find most exciting. Wall art isn't just a finishing touch you add once the "real" decorating is done — it can be the very starting point from which your entire colour palette is built.

I always recommend choosing your key piece of wall art before you choose your paint colour. A print or canvas you genuinely love already contains a perfectly balanced colour palette. All you have to do is lift those colours out and apply them to the room around it.

[[IMG|wall-art-prints-dining-room-colour-palette|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, warm natural palette, contemporary British home styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor welcome — a ceramic wall shelf with small plants, a woven wall hanging, wall sconces. Scene: A dining room where the colour palette is clearly inspired by art and decor — warm sage green walls, terracotta ceramic tableware on a round table, a mustard linen table runner, and a dried flower arrangement in earthenware. The walls feature a macramé hanging and two ceramic wall plates, not framed pictures. A mixed-race couple — a South Asian woman and a white man, both in their 30s — are standing near the table together looking at paint swatches, comparing them to the ceramic tableware in a natural, candid way.]]

How to Pull a Colour Palette from a Piece of Art

  • Identify the dominant colour in the artwork — this becomes your wall or furniture colour.
  • Find the secondary colour (usually in the mid-tones of the piece) — this works well for textiles like curtains or a rug.
  • Use the accent or highlight colour from the artwork for small decor pieces: candles, ceramics, vases.
  • If the art contains a neutral (cream, warm white, grey), use that for trim, skirting boards, and ceiling.
  • Don't match the art exactly to the wall colour — a small amount of contrast between art and wall makes both look better.
  • Hang art at eye level when seated (around 140–150cm from the floor to the centre of the piece) in a dining room specifically.

The mistake I always see is people buying art to match their existing room rather than letting it lead the room. I had a client who'd repainted her dining room three times in two years trying to find the right colour. Then she bought a large botanical print she adored — and we built the whole room around it in shades of warm cream, deep sage and rust. She hasn't wanted to change anything since.

Pro Tip: If you already have art on your dining room walls, take a photograph of it and use a free colour-picker tool online to identify the exact hex codes of its main colours. You can then take those codes to a paint supplier and find the closest match — it's a far more precise method than eyeballing it.
[[PRODUCT|large-format botanical wall art prints for the dining room]]

Pairing Wall Decor with Specific Paint Colours

Certain paint colours have very natural partners when it comes to wall decor, and knowing those combinations in advance saves an enormous amount of trial and error. It's less about rules and more about understanding contrast, warmth, and visual balance.

The key question is always: does the wall decor need to stand out against the wall, or blend harmoniously with it? Both can work — but you need to decide which effect you're going for before you start hanging things.

[[IMG|wall-decor-paired-with-paint-colours-dining-room|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, contemporary British home styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor welcome — macramé, ceramic wall plates, mirror, shelves with ceramics and plants. Scene: A dining room with deep dusty blue-green walls. On the walls hang a large round rattan mirror, two ceramic wall plates in cream and warm terracotta tones, and a small shelf holding a trailing plant and two cream beeswax candles. A dark wood dining table is set simply with linen napkins and a natural stone candle holder. A Black British man in his early 50s stands by the shelf, adjusting a small plant pot in a relaxed, candid pose.]]

Paint Colour to Wall Decor Pairings

  • Deep sage green: Pairs beautifully with natural rattan mirrors, terracotta ceramic wall plates, and dried botanicals in earthy frames.
  • Midnight navy: Works brilliantly with gold or brass-finish wall sconces, cream-toned macramé, and warm-toned abstract wall prints in amber or ochre.
  • Warm terracotta: Looks stunning with woven hanging decor, dark wood shelf brackets, and cream or off-white ceramic pieces.
  • Soft warm white: A blank canvas — go for statement pieces with bold colour, natural textures like rattan or linen, or a gallery wall with warm wood frames.
  • Charcoal or near-black: Pair with brushed silver or pewter-finish sconces, light-toned art subjects with warm frames, and trailing plants in white or cream pots.
  • Dusty blush or mauve: Complement with vintage-style botanical prints, gilded-edge mirrors, and soft natural linen wall hangings.
Real Example: A client had painted her dining room in a deep inky green and then bought stark white ceramic wall plates to hang — and the contrast was so harsh it looked clinical. We swapped them for warm cream and terracotta versions instead, and the whole wall came to life. Matching the warmth or coolness of your decor to the underlying tone of your paint colour is the detail that ties a room together.
[[PRODUCT|dining room wall art prints in ochre amber and warm tones]]

Colour Palette Ideas by Dining Room Aesthetic

Your dining room's overall aesthetic — the style and design language you're working with — should shape your colour choices as much as the practical factors of light and size. These days there are so many distinct aesthetics to draw from, and each one has a really clear colour language once you know what to look for.

I find it helpful to identify one primary aesthetic and one secondary one, then let those two inform your colour and decor decisions. It stops a room feeling like it's from nowhere — or everywhere at once.

[[IMG|dining-room-aesthetic-colour-palettes|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor welcome — minimal ceramic wall-hung shelf, a single trailing plant, a simple wooden peg rail. Scene: A Japandi-aesthetic dining room in warm white and warm stone tones with a low natural oak table, boucle upholstered chairs in warm cream, a single linen pendant light, and a simple ceramic jug on the table with a single stem. The walls are bare warm white plaster with a small wooden peg rail holding a linen tote. A Japanese woman in her 30s is carefully arranging a single dried flower stem in the ceramic jug, serene and candid.]]

Colour Palettes by Dining Room Aesthetic

  • Minimalist: Warm white, light stone, pale greige. One deliberate accent — a single warm mustard or muted terracotta. Avoid clutter in colour and objects alike.
  • Japandi: Stone, warm cream, warm white, soft sand, with natural wood and muted sage as secondary tones. Nothing high-contrast or bright.
  • Maximalist: Deep, jewel-toned walls (teal, plum, forest green) with layered pattern, gold accents, and rich mixed colours across textiles and art. Clashing is encouraged — deliberately.
  • Cottagecore / country: Warm cream, sage, duck egg blue, warm yellow. Mismatched china, dried flowers, woven textiles, and hand-painted ceramics are your best friends.
  • Industrial: Charcoal, warm grey, raw brick tones, with black metal accents and aged warm-toned wood. Avoid anything soft or pastel.
  • Coastal / nautical: Sandy cream, driftwood grey, soft aqua, navy. Natural textures like seagrass, linen and rattan work alongside muted blues and warm whites.
  • Eclectic / bohemian: Rich saffron, rust, dusty rose, teal, ochre. Layer patterns, mix metals, and embrace art from multiple sources and styles.
Pro Tip: If you're going maximalist, choose one colour as a "hero" that repeats at least three times throughout the room — on a wall, in a textile, and in a decor object. That repetition is what stops a maximalist room from looking chaotic and makes it look curated instead.
[[PRODUCT|maximalist eclectic colourful wall art prints for the dining room]]

Budget-Friendly Ways to Introduce Colour Through Art and Accessories

Paint is brilliant, but it's not the only way to bring colour into a dining room — and for renters, or anyone who's just not ready to commit to a full repaint, art and accessories can do an enormous amount of the heavy lifting.

The principle is simple: colour reads in a room regardless of what surface it's on. A set of terracotta ceramic vases on a sideboard will read as "terracotta dining room" almost as strongly as terracotta walls would. And it costs a fraction of the price, with none of the hassle.

[[IMG|budget-colour-through-art-and-accessories-dining-room|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, contemporary British home styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor welcome — macramé hangings, woven wall baskets, a mirror. Scene: A rented or budget dining room with plain white walls that look warm and colourful due to accessories — a mustard yellow rug under a round table, terracotta ceramics on the table, a woven macramé wall hanging in earthy tones, a large round rattan mirror, green trailing plants in cream pots, and linen cushions on the dining chairs in dusty blush and sage. A young Latina woman in her late 20s crouches by the sideboard arranging ceramic pots, candid and natural.]]

Budget Colour Ideas Without Paint

  • Hang a large print or gallery wall as a focal point — even two or three coordinating prints together create a strong colour statement.
  • Layer a colourful rug under the dining table — it defines the zone and introduces colour at floor level without touching the walls.
  • Replace plain dining chair cushions or pads with ones in a bold or contrasting colour.
  • Group ceramic vases, jugs, or candle holders on a sideboard in two or three complementary colours for a curated look.
  • Swap out your pendant light shade for one in a coloured material — terracotta rattan, sage green cotton, or warm amber glass all add instant colour overhead.
  • Invest in coloured linen napkins and a tablecloth — it's the most flexible and cheapest way to shift the colour story of a room seasonally.
  • Add a large woven basket, wall hanging, or macramé piece for warm earthy tones without any commitment.

I always tell renters and first-time decorators: start with a rug and a print. Those two things alone can completely transform the feel of a room. I once turned a completely generic cream-box dining room into something that felt genuinely personal just using a sage green rug, a mustard linen pendant shade, and two large botanical prints on opposite walls. The total spend was less than most people spend on a single tin of specialist paint.

[[PRODUCT|gallery wall prints set for the dining room in coordinating tones]]
Pro Tip: When you're using art and accessories as your main source of colour, pick ONE colour to repeat at least three times across different objects — once in the rug, once in a ceramic, once in a textile. That repetition is what makes a room look styled rather than random.
[[PRODUCT|rattan pendant light shade in earthy or warm tones for dining rooms]]

Seasonal and Trend-Led Dining Room Palettes for Right Now

Colour trends in interiors change more slowly than fashion — a dining room you paint this year isn't going out of style next season. That said, there are some genuinely beautiful directions gaining momentum right now, and a lot of them translate really well into dining rooms specifically.

The good news is that even if you're not ready to repaint, most of these trends can be introduced through textiles, accessories, and art — which means you can stay current without committing to a full decorating project.

[[IMG|seasonal-trend-dining-room-colour-palette|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, warm earthy palette, contemporary British home styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor welcome — a seasonal dried wreath, a woven wall hanging, ceramic wall plates. Scene: A dining room styled for an autumnal seasonal palette — warm burnt sienna walls, a round table set with deep amber candles, warm ochre linen napkins, a ceramic pumpkin-shaped vessel in the centre, and dried wheat and eucalyptus in a terracotta vase. Warm pendant lighting glows overhead. A mixed-race family of four — a white woman, a Black man, and two children around 6 and 9 — are sitting down to a meal together, candid and natural.]]

Current and Trending Colour Directions for Dining Rooms

  • Warm earthy tones: Terracotta, warm sand, raw clay, and rust are at the height of their popularity right now — and they photograph beautifully too.
  • Moody deep greens: From sage to forest to emerald, green continues to be the most versatile and trend-resistant colour in interiors.
  • Warm off-whites and putty tones: The move away from cool, stark whites continues — warm plaster tones and limewash finishes are leading the way.
  • Chocolate brown and caramel: Rich warm browns are having a genuine moment in interiors right now — paired with cream and brass, they feel luxurious without being cold.
  • Seasonal shifts through accessories: Keep a neutral or warm base year-round and swap out textiles, candles, and ceramics seasonally — richer tones in autumn and winter, lighter fresher ones in spring and summer.
Pro Tip: For an easy seasonal refresh, keep a box of dining room accessories in seasonal colours. A set of deep burgundy linen napkins and amber glass candle holders can completely shift a room from summer-fresh to autumn-cosy in under ten minutes. It's one of the most cost-effective decorating habits I know.
[[PRODUCT|autumnal and earthy-toned wall art prints for dining rooms]]

Inspiring Dining Room Colour Styles: From Japandi to Maximalist

Sometimes seeing a room rather than reading about it is what finally clicks everything into place. Below you'll find a curated selection of dining room colour looks across a range of styles and palettes — from calm and minimal to rich and layered.

Visual Inspiration

Explore complementary design ideas on our Home Decor by Trend page:

  • Modern Contemporary Home Decor Trend - Bold palettes for modern dining
  • Cosy Minimalism Home Decor Trend - Calm neutral tones dining rooms
  • Eclectic Maximalist Home Decor Trend - Vibrant layered colour dining inspiration

More About Building a Complete Dining Room Colour Palette

A great dining room colour palette is never just about the paint — it's the full picture of colour, texture, light, and layers working together.

If you want to see how professional designers and colour experts approach this, it's worth exploring resources that go deep on the topic. For instance, The 24 Best Dining Room Colors, According to Designers offers a really strong visual reference for how different colours read in real dining rooms across a range of styles — useful for pressure-testing your own ideas before you commit.

What I'd add to any expert advice is this: always start with something you already love — a piece of art, a fabric, a ceramic — and build outward from there. The palette that emerges will feel coherent precisely because it's rooted in something real and personal to you, rather than assembled from trend boards and paint charts alone.

WATCH: 10 Perfect Dining Room Paint Colors – Ideas & Inspiration

Your Dining Room, Your Colour Story

If there's one thing I hope you take away from all of this, it's that choosing a dining room colour palette doesn't have to feel like a high-stakes decision. Start small, start with what you love, and let the room evolve naturally from there.

You don't need to do everything at once. A rug and a print can transform a space. A painted sideboard can change the whole conversation. And when you're ready to paint, you'll be doing it with real confidence because the palette will already feel like yours — not something you borrowed from a paint brand's catalogue.

The most memorable dining rooms I've ever worked in weren't the ones with the biggest budgets or the most perfect colour combinations. They were the ones that felt genuinely lived-in and personal. That's always the goal.

So tell me — is there one colour you've always wanted to try in your dining room but haven't quite had the courage to go for yet? I'd love to know what's holding you back.

A warm rattan pendant light glows overhead. The overall palette is sage, terracotta, warm cream and mustard — layered and inviting.

how do i plan a gallery wall layout?.bodyHtml:
Gallery wall layout planning doesn't have to be intimidating — once you break it down into clear steps, it's genuinely one of the most satisfying things you can do to transform a blank wall into something that feels truly personal and intentional.

By Mae Osz | Interior Design Consultant & Home Decor Expert with 12+ years of experience.

Have you ever stood in front of a bare wall, a stack of frames at your feet, and completely frozen? I've been there — and so have nearly every client I've worked with. The good news is that getting your wall art arranged beautifully is far less about natural talent and far more about having a simple, reliable process to follow.

Quick answer: To plan a gallery wall layout, start by choosing your wall and deciding on a rough shape (grid, organic cluster, or salon style). Gather your frames and art, then use paper templates taped to the wall to map out the arrangement before you put a single nail in. From there, measure carefully, mark your hanging points, and work from the centre outwards.

Gallery wall layout planning is essentially the process of deciding how multiple pieces of art, photos, or decor will be arranged on a wall in a way that feels balanced, considered, and visually cohesive — rather than just randomly hammered up. It's a skill that draws on a mix of basic measurement, a feel for proportion, and a bit of personal style. If you're looking for unique wall art to anchor your display, or want to pull in some unique home decor pieces to add texture and personality, having a proper plan in place first makes all the difference.

List of Contents

  • How to Plan a Gallery Wall Layout Step by Step
  • Best Gallery Wall Arrangements and Spacing Tips
  • How to Choose Frames and Art Sizes for a Gallery Wall
  • How to Measure and Mark Your Wall Before Hanging
  • Tools and Templates to Plan Your Gallery Wall Layout
  • Printable or DIY Paper Template Method for Planning Without Software
  • Room-by-Room Gallery Wall Layout Ideas
  • Common Gallery Wall Layout Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
  • How to Mix Art Styles, Frames, and Mediums Cohesively
  • Gallery Wall Style Inspiration
  • Further Reading on Gallery Wall Design
  • Ready to Start Your Gallery Wall?

How to Plan a Gallery Wall Layout Step by Step

The key to successful gallery wall layout planning is to never rush straight to the hammer. Think of it like baking — prep is everything. A clear sequence makes the whole process feel manageable, even if this is your very first time.

Here's the exact order I walk every client through, whether they're working with two pieces or twenty-two.

[[IMG|gallery-wall-layout-planning-step-by-step|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome — shelves, a macramé hanging, wall sconces. Style the walls naturally and lived-in. A bright, airy living room with a large cream-painted feature wall. A wooden coffee table is visible and a soft linen sofa in the foreground. Paper templates in various sizes are taped to the wall in a cluster arrangement, with a tape measure and pencil resting on the floor nearby. Include one person: a Black British woman in her early 30s, casually dressed, standing back from the wall with her arms folded, studying the paper arrangement thoughtfully in a natural candid pose.]]

Step-by-step process

  • Step 1 — Pick your wall. Choose a wall that has enough uninterrupted space. Avoid walls broken up by lots of doors, windows, or radiators unless you're working around them intentionally.
  • Step 2 — Define your shape. Decide if you want a structured grid, a loose organic cluster, or a wide horizontal arrangement (great for hallways). Sketch it roughly on paper first.
  • Step 3 — Collect all your pieces. Lay everything you might use flat on the floor in front of the wall. Include frames, canvases, mirrors, and any wall-hung objects.
  • Step 4 — Edit ruthlessly. More pieces doesn't always mean better. Pull out anything that doesn't feel right and set it aside without guilt.
  • Step 5 — Plan on the floor first. Rearrange your pieces on the floor until you love the layout. Take a photo so you don't forget it.
  • Step 6 — Transfer to the wall using paper templates. Cut paper to each frame size and tape them to the wall. Step back regularly to assess.
  • Step 7 — Mark, hang, and adjust. Only once you're happy with the paper arrangement do you start marking hanging points and putting nails in.

I once helped a client who'd already put 14 nails in a wall before calling me — none of the pieces were level and the grouping felt chaotic. We stripped it all back, spent 20 minutes with paper templates, and rehung everything in under an hour. The paper stage is never wasted time.

Pro Tip: Take a photo of your floor arrangement before you touch the wall. It's your cheat sheet for the whole hanging process — you'll thank yourself later.
[[PRODUCT|black and white photography wall art prints for gallery walls]]

Best Gallery Wall Arrangements and Spacing Tips

There are a handful of tried-and-tested arrangement styles that tend to work in most spaces, and knowing which one suits your wall is half the battle. The spacing between pieces is just as important as the arrangement itself — too wide and it reads as separate pictures rather than a cohesive display.

As a general rule, I recommend keeping gaps between frames between 5 and 10 cm. Tighter gaps (around 5 cm) give a maximalist, collected feel. Wider gaps (around 8 to 10 cm) feel more curated and airy.

[[IMG|gallery-wall-arrangement-styles-comparison|3:2|infographic|Clean minimal educational infographic, plain WHITE background, photoreal, all text solid BLACK. A short centred title near the top reading "Gallery Wall Arrangement Styles". Then three clearly labelled side-by-side visual examples: 1) a neat symmetrical grid of equally sized rectangles labelled "Grid / Symmetrical", 2) a loose organic cluster of mixed-size rectangles in different orientations labelled "Salon / Organic Cluster", 3) a single horizontal row of frames at the same height labelled "Horizontal Line". Minimal words, generous white space, nothing near the edges. No people, no watermarks.]]

Popular gallery wall arrangement styles

  • Grid layout: All frames the same size, evenly spaced in rows and columns. Clean, modern, and very satisfying if you like order.
  • Salon wall: Mixed sizes and orientations, filling a large area of wall in a loose, collected way. Works brilliantly in living rooms and stairwells.
  • Horizontal line: A single row of frames at the same height — perfect for hallways, above a sofa, or along a staircase landing.
  • Triptych: Three pieces (often the same size) displayed side by side, usually as a matching set or a panoramic image split across frames.
  • Asymmetric cluster: A central anchor piece (usually larger) with smaller pieces arranged around it — great for beginners because the anchor gives you a starting point.

Spacing guidance at a glance

Arrangement Style Recommended Gap Best For
Grid / Symmetrical 5–7 cm Modern, minimal spaces
Salon / Organic Cluster 5–8 cm (varied) Living rooms, eclectic homes
Horizontal Line 8–12 cm Hallways, above furniture
Asymmetric Cluster 5–8 cm Beginners, feature walls
Triptych 3–5 cm Bedrooms, dining rooms
Pro Tip: If your arrangement feels too scattered, try bringing all the pieces 2 cm closer together. It's surprising how much tighter gaps unify a display.
[[PRODUCT|abstract art prints for salon-style gallery walls]]

How to Choose Frames and Art Sizes for a Gallery Wall

Getting the mix of frame sizes and art proportions right is what separates a gallery wall that looks considered from one that just looks busy. You don't need everything to match — but you do need a logic running through it.

A good rule of thumb is to have one or two larger "anchor" pieces (around A2 or bigger), a few medium pieces (A3 or similar), and then a handful of smaller accent pieces. That variety of scale creates visual rhythm.

[[IMG|choosing-frames-art-sizes-gallery-wall|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome — a simple shelf with small objects, a hanging plant. Style the walls naturally and lived-in. A living room floor scene with multiple frames of different sizes laid out flat, ranging from small square frames to large rectangular ones. A tape measure and a pencil are nearby. Include one person: a South Asian man in his late 30s, kneeling on the floor and arranging the frames in a thoughtful candid pose.]]

Frame and art size selection tips

  • Start with an anchor piece. A large print or canvas (A2, 50x70 cm, or bigger) gives the eye a natural focal point and anchors the rest of the arrangement.
  • Vary your orientations. Mix portrait, landscape, and square frames to keep things visually interesting — avoid having everything the same way up.
  • Frame styles don't have to match exactly. But they should share at least one common element — colour (all black, all natural wood), finish (all matte, all thin profile), or material.
  • Consider matting. A wide white or cream mat inside a frame makes smaller prints feel more substantial and adds breathing room.
  • Group odd numbers. Collections of three, five, or seven pieces tend to feel more natural than even numbers in organic arrangements.
  • Think about the overall shape. Whether your final grouping forms a rectangle, a square, or a loose oval, having a clear outer boundary makes it feel intentional.

One of my favourite tricks when a client has frames in different finishes is to unify them with a consistent mat colour. I did this in a terraced house in Bristol — we had gold frames, black frames, and natural oak all living together. White mats throughout tied the whole wall together instantly.

Pro Tip: Lay all your potential frames on the floor and photograph them from above. That bird's-eye shot often reveals size imbalances you simply can't see when you're standing over them.
[[PRODUCT|minimalist line art prints for bedroom gallery walls]]

How to Measure and Mark Your Wall Before Hanging

This is the step most people skip — and it's the reason so many gallery walls end up wonky or lopsided. Proper measuring before you pick up the hammer saves you from a wall full of unnecessary holes and a lot of frustration.

The goal is to find the centre point of your planned arrangement and work outwards from there, rather than starting from one edge and hoping for the best.

[[IMG|measuring-marking-wall-gallery-layout|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor welcome — a wall sconce, a small floating shelf. Style the walls naturally and lived-in. A close-up scene of a freshly plastered white wall with paper templates taped in place. A spirit level is pressed against the templates, and a pencil mark is being made on the wall. A tape measure is stretched horizontally. Include one person: a white British woman in her 40s, wearing a casual shirt, focused and precise in her movements, in a natural candid pose.]]

How to measure and mark accurately

  • Find the centre of your wall space. Measure the width of the wall (or your designated hanging area) and divide by two. Mark this lightly with pencil.
  • Decide on the hanging height. The centre of your gallery wall arrangement should sit at approximately eye level — usually around 145 to 155 cm from the floor. If it's above a sofa or console, position the bottom of the arrangement 20 to 25 cm above the furniture.
  • Account for the hanging hardware. Every frame's hanging hook sits a few centimetres down from the top of the frame. Measure this gap on each frame and factor it into your mark on the wall.
  • Use a spirit level religiously. Even a slight tilt is noticeable once a frame is on the wall. Check every mark horizontally and vertically.
  • Mark lightly in pencil. Never mark in pen or marker. Pencil wipes off easily — pen does not.
  • Double-check before nailing. Once all marks are on the wall, step back and assess before you put a single nail in. Take a photo and check it against your floor layout photo.
Real Example: I had a client who hung an entire row of frames 10 cm too high because she measured from the top of her sofa rather than the floor. The row sat so high it looked disconnected from the furniture. We rehung everything and the difference was immediate — it anchored the sofa beautifully.

Tools and Templates to Plan Your Gallery Wall Layout

You don't need expensive software or a professional to plan a great gallery wall. But having the right tools to hand makes the process quicker, more accurate, and — honestly — more enjoyable.

Whether you're going fully analogue or using a digital app, having some kind of planning tool means you can experiment freely without committing to holes in your wall.

[[IMG|tools-templates-gallery-wall-planning|3:2|infographic|Clean minimal educational infographic, plain WHITE background, photoreal, all text solid BLACK. A short centred title near the top reading "Gallery Wall Planning Toolkit". Below, a simple labelled icon-style flat-lay showing six essential tools arranged clearly: a tape measure, a spirit level, a pencil, sheets of brown paper or newspaper, painter's tape, and a hammer. Each item has a short label beneath it. Minimal words, generous white space, nothing near the edges. No people, no watermarks.]]

Essential tools for gallery wall planning

  • Tape measure: Non-negotiable. You'll use it for measuring wall space, frame dimensions, and hanging hardware distances.
  • Spirit level: Essential for straight lines and level rows. A small torpedo level works well in tight spaces.
  • Pencil and eraser: For marking the wall temporarily. Always pencil, never pen.
  • Painter's tape: Use it to tape paper templates to the wall without damaging the paint.
  • Brown paper or newspaper: For creating DIY paper templates of each frame (more on this below).
  • Scissors: To cut paper templates to the exact frame dimensions.
  • Hammer and picture hooks: The final step — but these only come out once everything else is decided.
  • A smartphone camera: Invaluable for photographing your floor layout and wall templates to compare progress.

Digital planning tools worth knowing

  • Simple grid paper sketches (old-school but genuinely effective — I still use this).
  • Free room planner apps that let you map out wall arrangements to scale.
  • The camera on your phone paired with a photo editing app — tape a grid to your wall photo and sketch in rough frame outlines.
Pro Tip: Painter's tape is also useful for marking the outer boundary of your planned arrangement directly on the wall — it gives you a clear visual frame to work within before you add any paper templates.
[[PRODUCT|gallery wall hanging strips and picture hooks set]]

Printable or DIY Paper Template Method for Planning Without Software

This is genuinely my favourite method and the one I recommend to every single client who asks me how to plan a gallery wall layout without tools or apps. It costs almost nothing, it's incredibly accurate, and it means you can move things around freely until everything feels right.

All you need is brown parcel paper or a stack of old newspapers, a pencil, scissors, and some painter's tape.

[[IMG|diy-paper-template-gallery-wall-method|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor welcome — a macramé hanging, a small shelf. Style the walls naturally and lived-in. A warm, light-filled living room. Multiple brown paper templates of various sizes are taped to a white wall using painter's tape, arranged in an asymmetric cluster. One template is being repositioned. A pencil is tucked behind the ear of the person. Include one person: a mixed-race woman in her late 20s, standing on a small step stool reaching up to reposition a large paper template, in a natural candid pose.]]

How to create and use paper templates

  • Measure each frame. Get the exact width and height of every piece you plan to hang, including any frame border.
  • Cut paper to each size. Lay your paper flat, measure and mark the dimensions, then cut. Label each one in pencil so you know which frame it represents.
  • Mark the hanging point on each template. On the back of each paper template, mark where the nail or hook will sit — this is the distance from the top of the frame to the hanging hardware. This is crucial for accurate placement.
  • Tape everything to the wall. Start with your central or largest piece and work outwards. Use painter's tape at the corners — it peels off cleanly.
  • Step back and assess. Walk away, come back, and look again with fresh eyes. Move templates around freely until you're completely happy.
  • Mark through the template. Once satisfied, push a pencil through the marked hanging point on each template to transfer the nail position directly onto the wall. Remove the templates and nail straight into the marks.

The first time I tried this method myself — years before I became a professional — I was absolutely convinced I didn't need it. I thought I could just eyeball it. Reader, I had seven unnecessary holes in my dining room wall by the end of that afternoon. The paper template method has been sacred to me ever since.

Pro Tip: Use a different coloured pencil or a small cross to mark hanging points on your paper templates — it makes them far easier to spot when you're ready to transfer them to the wall.
[[PRODUCT|botanical art prints for hallway gallery walls]]

Room-by-Room Gallery Wall Layout Ideas

The best gallery wall layout for a living room is often completely wrong for a bedroom or hallway — and that's perfectly fine. Each room has its own mood, its own scale, and its own practical constraints. Knowing what works where saves a lot of trial and error.

Here's how I approach it room by room, based on what consistently works for the spaces I style.

[[IMG|room-by-room-gallery-wall-ideas|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor welcome — wall sconces, shelves, hanging plants, mirrors. Style the walls naturally and lived-in. A split-scene editorial image showing three distinct domestic spaces side by side: a bright living room with a large linen sofa; a calm bedroom with a low platform bed and linen bedding; and a narrow hallway with a console table and a vase of dried flowers. Include one person: an East Asian man in his early 40s, visible in the hallway section, walking through in a natural candid mid-step pose.]]

Living room

  • Choose a large anchor piece — at least A2 — to establish visual weight.
  • A salon wall (floor-to-ceiling if you're feeling bold) works brilliantly on a chimney breast or behind a sofa.
  • Include at least one larger canvas or oversized print to balance smaller pieces.
  • The bottom of the arrangement should sit roughly 20 to 25 cm above your sofa back.

Bedroom

  • Above the headboard is the classic position — centre the arrangement over the bed, not the wall.
  • Keep it calm and cohesive: fewer pieces, a limited colour palette, and a more relaxed arrangement style than the living room.
  • Avoid hanging heavy frames directly above your head. Opt for lightweight prints or canvas over metal-framed works above a bed.
  • A simple triptych or a gentle organic cluster of three to five pieces works beautifully here.

Hallway

  • Hallways reward a horizontal line arrangement — a row of frames at consistent eye level draws the eye down the corridor.
  • Keep the depth in mind: hallways are narrow, so pieces should be easy to appreciate at close range. Detailed photography or bold graphic prints work well.
  • Use the wall on one side only — doing both sides can feel claustrophobic in a narrow space.
  • Staircase walls are perfect for a tall, staggered diagonal arrangement that follows the line of the stairs.
Real Example: I styled a narrow Victorian hallway for a family who wanted to display their travel photography. We chose a diagonal staggered line following the staircase, all in matching thin black frames, with consistent spacing. It completely transformed what had been a dark, overlooked space into something the family genuinely loved walking past every day.
[[PRODUCT|travel and landscape photography wall art prints]] [[PRODUCT|rattan wall mirror for hallway decor]]

Common Gallery Wall Layout Mistakes and How to Avoid Them

There are a few gallery wall errors I see so often that I could spot them from across the street. The good news is that every single one of them is avoidable once you know what to look for.

Here are the mistakes I always see — and exactly how to fix them.

[[IMG|common-gallery-wall-mistakes-avoid|3:2|infographic|Clean minimal educational infographic, plain WHITE background, photoreal, all text solid BLACK. A short centred title near the top reading "Common Gallery Wall Mistakes". Below, five labelled side-by-side icon-style illustrations, each showing a simple mistake: 1) frames too small labelled "Art Too Small for the Wall", 2) frames spaced too far apart labelled "Gaps Too Wide", 3) all frames the same size labelled "No Size Variation", 4) frames all hung too high labelled "Hung Too High", 5) mismatched frames with no common element labelled "No Cohesion". Minimal words, generous white space, nothing near the edges. No people, no watermarks.]]

Mistakes and their fixes

  • Mistake: Hanging everything too high. Art should be centred at eye level, not picture-rail height. Fix: Measure to 145 to 155 cm from the floor to the centre of your arrangement.
  • Mistake: Choosing art that's too small for the wall. A tiny cluster of small frames on a large wall looks lost. Fix: Scale up, or add more pieces to fill the space properly.
  • Mistake: Gaps that are too large. Wide spacing makes a gallery wall read as individual pictures, not a cohesive display. Fix: Pull pieces to within 5 to 8 cm of each other.
  • Mistake: No visual anchor. A wall of similarly sized pieces lacks a focal point. Fix: Add one significantly larger piece as the centrepiece and arrange the rest around it.
  • Mistake: No cohesion between frames. A mix of gold, black, wood, and white frames with no common thread looks accidental. Fix: Unify with matching mat colours, a shared finish, or a consistent frame profile.
  • Mistake: Skipping the planning stage and going straight to the hammer. This is the one I see most often. Fix: Always use paper templates — always.
Pro Tip: If you're unsure whether your frames have enough visual cohesion, photograph them laid on a white floor and look at the image in black and white. If they still feel cohesive in greyscale, you're in good shape.

How to Mix Art Styles, Frames, and Mediums Cohesively

One of the most common questions I get is "can I mix photography with illustration? Can I put a canvas next to a framed print?" The answer is always yes — but you need a unifying thread. Without one, a mixed gallery wall risks looking like a car boot sale rather than a curated display.

Cohesion doesn't mean everything matching. It means everything belonging. Here's how to achieve that.

[[IMG|mixing-art-styles-frames-mediums-gallery-wall|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor welcome — a macramé wall hanging, a shelf with ceramic objects, a wall-mounted sconce with warm light. Style the walls naturally and lived-in. A calm, neutral sitting room with warm white walls. A wooden console table below the wall area with a ceramic vase and a small trailing plant. The wall shows a variety of different textures and materials — a woven wall hanging, a small ceramic wall-mounted plaque, a small decorative mirror — but no framed art. Include one person: a Black British man in his 50s, standing beside the console table, holding a small object and considering the wall arrangement, in a candid natural pose.]]

How to create cohesion across mixed pieces

  • Choose a colour palette and stick to it. Your art doesn't have to be the same style, but if the dominant tones are consistent — say, dusty greens, warm creams, and terracotta — the wall will feel connected.
  • Pick a unifying frame element. All black frames, all thin profiles, all natural wood, or all matte finishes. You can mix frame styles as long as they share one consistent trait.
  • Mix mediums with intention. Photography next to illustration next to a small mirror works — but try to balance them across the arrangement so one type doesn't cluster on one side.
  • Use matting to level the playing field. A consistent mat colour (usually white or off-white) inside varied frames creates a visual rhythm that ties everything together.
  • Vary texture, not colour. A canvas print, a framed watercolour, and a linen-mounted photograph can all sit happily together if their colours are complementary.
  • Add one wild card piece. A small mirror, a mounted ceramic, or a wall-hanging object adds personality without disrupting cohesion — as long as it shares the colour palette.

I always tell clients: think of your gallery wall like a well-dressed outfit. You don't need everything to match, but you need one strong thread pulling it together — like a belt that picks up the colour of your shoes. Find that thread and hold onto it.

Pro Tip: Before buying new frames, hold what you already have up to the wall in different combinations. You might already have the cohesion you need — it's often just about editing out the pieces that break the thread.

Gallery Wall Style Inspiration: Looks and Themes That Actually Work

Sometimes the hardest part isn't the planning — it's knowing what direction to take aesthetically. Looking at different style approaches can unlock exactly what you've been trying to articulate about your own space.

Here's a quick look at some of the most popular and enduring gallery wall themes I work with regularly.

Visual Inspiration

Further Reading on Gallery Wall Design

There's a lot of advice out there on gallery walls, but not all of it is grounded in practical, real-world experience.

One resource I consistently point people towards is HGTV's 7 Tips for Creating the Perfect Gallery Wall, which backs up the principle that your largest piece should anchor the arrangement — something I've found to be true in virtually every gallery wall I've planned. Combining that kind of foundational advice with the practical paper template method and room-specific thinking covered in this guide gives you everything you need to get it right first time.

WATCH: How to Create a Gallery Wall

WATCH: The Ultimate Guide to a Stunning Gallery Wall

Ready to Start Your Gallery Wall?

Planning a gallery wall really does come down to one thing: taking the time to plan before you pick up the hammer. Once you have a clear arrangement mapped out in paper templates, the rest follows naturally and quickly.

Start small if you need to — even three pieces arranged thoughtfully above a console table or a bedside table is a gallery wall. There's no minimum. And as your confidence grows, so can your display.
